In my next build, my plan is to dual-boot between Windows 10 and Ubuntu-based Linux, with two separate drives to hold their main systems and a shared drive to store Linux games (Steam library, Wine drive), PC games (Steam library), and other PC programs. What should be known about sharing a single NTFS drive between Windows and Linux?
Using a shared drive between Linux and Win10?

You could have a single NTFS drive store files, but you wouldn't be able to have both OSes run games from the same files because the operating systems are different and therefore the way games are installed and run is different. You will have to pick one OS (windows, I assume) to run the games and programs.
OP listed Linux games, and PC games (I'm guessing they mean Windows) separately. Their plan is solid.

He wanted to have a single drive that both OSes read the games and programs from. That won't work because programs run differently on the two operating systems. You're missing the point and thinking about something different. OP stated they want two separate Steam libraries. Linux library when on Linux, Windows library when using Windows. Not one library for both. They just both reside on the same hard drive. i.e. /mnt/shareddrive/linuxsteam and /mnt/shareddrive/windowssteam. That is perfectly fine, at least in Windows 7 or below and you don't use hibernation. See my other comment for issues with Windows 8 and possibly 10.

Because Steam on Linux is looking for Linux games. If your Steam was running in Wine, then it would look for the *.exe files.

I would try to run as many games in Linux as possible. That is to say, ones with native Linux compatibility or ones that can run in WINE. Smaller games would be kept on SSDs, while bigger games (GTA V, Fallout, etc.) would be put on the HDD. I would separate the Linux and Windows Steam libraries, of course.

Actually, after reading some, it looks like you don't want to do this with Windows 8, since it does some weird hybrid hibernation/shutdown when shutdown. Windows stores the file system states to disk when shutting down, and restores it when it boots, erasing any changes made in Ubuntu. I'm going to go ahead and guess that this behavior is in Windows 10 too. It might be a better idea to just have two partitions on the third drive. One EXT4 (or whatever other FS you want) for Linux, and one NTFS for Windows.

It's not a problem. In fact I always have 3 to 4 partitions not counting swap and recovery. 1 or 2 for files and two for OS's it means a lot less hassle if you need to install again. And it means I have a spare partition if I want to install a distro and see how it works for a month before wiping out my old distro.
Shared NTFS drives can cause problems, especially if you use hibernation (in Windows). A shared FAT32 drive might be better.
